prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I opened with fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B003) as my first choice, and I still think it is the strongest piece of pure theory on this list. After reading all eight opening ballots, however, I move my preferred configuration to the optical lattice clock (B041). It is the only candidate that six of eight members place in their top three, and the reasons given are the ones I find most persuasive: the idea has a clear origin (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice), the performance claims have been reproduced independently in several laboratories at the 1e-18 level, the interpretation is stable, and the attribution to two names is clean, which is rare on this list. It changed what can be measured, enabling relativistic-redshift tests over millimetre scales, constraints on constants and prospects for redefining the second. Of the candidates with a settled, well-confirmed physical picture it is the one where the credited names fit the three-person limit without forcing a hard cut.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a clock is a measurement achievement and a prize for it may read more as metrology than as a discovery about nature; the committee should say plainly whether it wants that. The lineage also overlaps with the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for ion control, so the citation must be drawn tightly around the lattice concept and its realization. Other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others named by colleagues) contributed to the clock programme and are outside the credited names, and the SI redefinition has not happened, which may argue for waiting. Finally, my own field is far from atomic clocks, so on the experimental systematics I rely on colleagues such as Eva Lindroth and Stefan Kroll.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest case where what can be measured, and how accurately, changed in kind, with a two-person credit drawn on the lattice concept and a stable, widely reproduced interpretation.
responses.response: I agree with this and it is the main reason I moved. I would add one qualification. Your caveat that Ye might be credited mainly through the comb and clock programme rather than the lattice clock alone is a real risk, and I think the citation should name the lattice clock explicitly so that it does not read as a second comb prize. I also thought the single-ion and comb lineage was the weakest point of the case, and your suggestion to draw the boundary on the lattice concept answers it well enough for me.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a bold instrumental achievement that opened neutrino astronomy, but concedes that allocating credit within a 300-plus collaboration, including the AMANDA pioneers, is the real difficulty.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube fourth for the same reason you describe. The instrument is remarkable, but individual credit is diffuse, and I said that any three-person credit is somewhat arbitrary. You propose two of three names and I used three; the difference shows how unsettled the allocation is. The TXS 0506+056 association at 3 to 4 sigma and the open question of the diffuse flux's origin also tell me the physical results are less deep than the instrument. I would not put this ahead of a candidate where the credit is clean, but I would not exclude it later if the source population firms up.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first: a flat-band prediction followed by decisive experiments, widely reproduced, with a fair theory-plus-experiment split, and timing appropriate for the originating discovery.
responses.response: I share your assessment of the science and I ranked it third. I think it is the most serious rival to the clock, and I list it as my first alternative. Where I differ is in weighing the unresolved pairing mechanism. You treat the core observations as stable enough; I agree on the existence of the correlated phases, but the interpretation is not yet settled and priority questions about earlier theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) remain, plus the role of Cao and Fatemi on the experimental side. For a prize the clock has a stronger record of stable interpretation. If the committee is willing to reward the platform rather than the mechanism, I would not oppose B017.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first and twisted bilayer graphene second, and for the lattice clock notes that overlap with earlier prizes on frequency combs and ion traps may weigh against novelty, while the redefinition of the second has not yet occurred.
responses.response: I take the novelty objection seriously but do not think it is decisive. The 2005 prize was for the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies; the lattice clock uses it to reach a many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free regime with an uncertainty that the earlier work did not give. That is a distinct invention. I accept the point that a redefinition of the second is not required for the clock to qualify, and that its arrival would only strengthen the case, so waiting does not seem to me necessary. I also take your caution on IceCube attribution as support for my own concern.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and notes that a future redefinition of the second might be a more natural moment, and that many strontium and ytterbium groups contributed besides the two credited names.
responses.response: I think the many-groups point is the strongest argument against any narrow credit, and I would answer it by relying on the lattice concept and its record-setting realization rather than the whole clock field. On timing I do not see a reason to tie the prize to the SI redefinition: the performance is already confirmed by independent clocks agreeing below 1e-18. I would value your view on whether the Katori-Ye pair is complete for the lattice concept, since you know the community better than I do.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a metrology invention rather than a discovery about nature, and how to word a citation that does not duplicate the 2005 comb prize.
Whether Katori and Ye fully capture the lattice-clock credit or whether other proposers and groups (Lemonde, Ludlow and others) would be seen as omitted.

For my own first choice, B003, priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Gallavotti, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert is unresolved, and no one else has ranked it, so I cannot say it would hold up as a configuration.
My recollection that the 2025 prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is unverified, and it bears on how I weigh B028.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my documented co-authors and institutional ties (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg) do not include any credited person for B041, B017 or B003. My work on statistical and stochastic physics is close in subject to B003, which I rank as an alternative, but I know of no personal tie to Jarzynski, Evans, Crooks or Seifert.
